notes:
I have gathered substantial material. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I wasn't able to access Catholic/Orthodox, Lutheran, or Methodist-specific sources, nor modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey, NET Bible notes) due to search/fetch limits, but I have rich material from the other traditions. Here are the notes:

---

## Genesis 33 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

Jacob, having wrestled with God at Peniel, now faces Esau. The dreaded meeting becomes a warm reconciliation. The brothers part peacefully; Jacob settles first at Succoth, then at Shechem in Canaan, where he buys land and builds an altar.

---

### vv. 1–2 — Jacob's Careful Arrangements

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming with 400 men.** After the night of wrestling, the crisis Jacob feared now arrives. He must trust God's promises of protection (Genesis 28:13–15; 31:3) now that the moment is upon him. (David Guzik, Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- **He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants.** Gill notes some think Jacob made four divisions, others three (the two handmaids together). The word for "divide" literally means to halve, so Gill suggests the two wives and their children in one company, the two handmaids and theirs in the other — done "partly for decency and partly for safety." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **He put the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.** The order reflects Jacob's degree of affection: handmaids least honoured, Rachel and Joseph most beloved. The Pulpit Commentary adds "or most beautiful (Bush)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Ellicott says Jacob "provided some small chance of escape for his wives and children, arranged according to their rank." — (from search excerpt)

- Constable notes: "This kind of ranking according to favoritism no doubt fed the jealousy over Joseph that later becomes an important element in the narrative. It must have been painful to the family to see that they were expendable." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

- Guzik says these preparations were "not necessarily examples of unbelief or reliance on human wisdom and strength," though the order shows Jacob openly favoured Rachel and Joseph. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Matthew Henry: "Jacob, having by prayer committed his case to God, went on his way. Come what will, nothing can come amiss to him whose heart is fixed, trusting in God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

**Denominational Distinctives:** No substantial divergence among traditions on these verses. All treat Jacob's arrangement as a mix of prudent caution and favouritism.

---

### v. 3 — Jacob Bows Seven Times

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Jacob himself went on ahead.** After being conquered by God (ch. 32), he now leads the procession — displaying change of character. He "chivalrously" puts himself in the place of danger (Pulpit). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- **Bowed to the ground seven times.** Not full prostration but bending the upper body parallel to the ground — "a mode of expressing deep reverence and respect, which may be seen to life in Oriental countries at the present day" (Pulpit). Gill adds that while bowing civilly to Esau as his elder brother, "religious adoration might be made to God; while he thus bowed to the ground, his heart might be going up to God in prayer." The Targum of Jonathan inserts: "praying, and asking mercies of the Lord, and bowed…" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- Ellicott: the sevenfold obeisance acknowledged Esau's superiority, "for the cause of the quarrel had been Jacob's usurpation of Esau's right of precedence as the first born." The bow is made "by bending the body forward with the arms crossed, and the right hand held over the heart." — (from search excerpt)

- Guzik: "Jacob already sent over gifts…and by this showed he didn't want to take anything materially from Esau. Then, by bowing down, he showed he was submitted to his brother and wanted no social power over him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- The Pulpit Commentary insists Jacob's conduct "was dictated neither by artful hypocrisy nor by unmanly timidity; but by true politeness and a sincere desire to conciliate." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

---

### v. 4 — Esau's Embrace: The Kiss and the Tears

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, and kissed him.** The sight of Esau running probably terrified Jacob — he thought his life would end. Instead, "God had worked in Esau, and he only wanted to bring a blessing to Jacob" (Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Gill compares it to the father of the prodigal son running to meet him (Luke 15:20), and notes the **puncta extraordinaria** (three extraordinary dots) placed by the Masoretes over the Hebrew word for "kissed him" (וַיִּשָּׁקֵהוּ). Jewish writers are divided: "some think that this points at the insincerity of Esau in kissing his brother when he hated him; others, on the contrary, to his sincerity and heartiness in it, and which was matter of admiration, that he…should have his heart so turned toward him, which must be owing to the power of God working upon his heart." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary elaborates that the puncta extraordinaria "seem to indicate either that in their judgment Esau was incapable of such fraternal affection (Delitzsch, Kalisch), or that the word was suspicious, Origen appearing not to have found it in his codices (Rosenmüller, Keil), unless indeed the conjecture be correct that the word was marked to draw attention to the power of God's grace in changing Esau's heart (Ainsworth)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Ellicott firmly rejects the sceptical reading: "Whatever may have been Esau's intention when he started, no sooner does he see his brother than the old times of their childhood return to his heart, and he is overcome with love…For such an ill-natured supposition there is no warrant whatsoever." — (from search excerpt)

- **And they both wept.** Esau wept from meeting his twin after 20+ years; Jacob's tears were "probably from relief that his brother had not murdered him and his family in revenge, as he had previously vowed (Genesis 27:41)" (Guzik). The LXX adds "both." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Matthew Henry: "God has the hearts of all men in his hands, and can turn them when and how he pleases. It is not in vain to trust in God, and to call upon him in the day of trouble." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

- Guzik adds: "Apparently, Esau and Jacob did not feel a need to discuss and resolve the past. God worked in both their hearts, and there was no need to discuss or argue over it all again. What was past was past." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Spurgeon, preaching on Jacob's prayer of ch. 32, notes this as its answer: "His brother 'Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.' So, beloved, trust ye in the Lord, and wait patiently for him, and your enemies shall become your friends." — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jacobs-model-prayer

**Denominational Distinctives:**

- The **Jewish Masoretic tradition** (the dots) raised suspicion about Esau's sincerity — some later rabbinic sources saw Esau as a typological enemy of Israel. Ellicott and most Christian commentators reject this reading.
- **Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist)** preaches this as evidence of God answering prayer and changing hearts — a sovereign work of grace. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jacobs-model-prayer

---

### vv. 5–7 — Introducing the Family

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Who are these with you?"** Esau noticed the women and children. Gill notes Jacob had made no mention of his wives and children when he sent messengers earlier (Genesis 32:5). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **"The children God has graciously given your servant."** Jacob speaks of his children as gifts of God, "instances and pledges of his favour," and "owns himself his servant" (Gill). Matthew Henry: "To this common question, Jacob spoke like himself, like a man whose eyes are ever directed towards the Lord." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary notes Jacob uses **Elohim** rather than **Jehovah** — possibly "to avoid reminding Esau of the blessing of Jehovah which had occasioned his absence" (Delitzsch, Keil), or because "Jehovah was exalted far above the level of Esau's superficial religion" (Hengstenberg). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- **The handmaids…Leah…Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed.** Joseph is mentioned before his mother Rachel. Gill says Joseph was "a child of little more than six years of age," and Rachel may have "present him to Esau…and teach him how to make his obeisance." Jarchi speculated Joseph took precedence to protect his mother's beauty from Esau's gaze, but the Pulpit calls this "as fanciful and far-fetched" as Lange's idea that the six-year-old "rushes confidently into the arms of his uncle." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

---

### vv. 8–9 — The Gift Refused

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"What do you mean by sending this whole company to meet me?"** Esau asks about the droves. He knew their purpose from the drovers but wanted to hear it from Jacob and have the opportunity to refuse (Gill). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **"To find favor in your sight, my lord."** Jacob's language is that of a subordinate to a superior.

- **"I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you."** Esau's Hebrew is "I have much" (רַב). The Pulpit Commentary remarks: "it is impossible not to admire the generous and affectionate disposition of Esau." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Guzik: Esau's peace and contentment "showed him to be a remarkably blessed man, though he did not receive the promise of the Abrahamic covenant." Quoting Spurgeon: "Although Esau did not receive the great blessing — the covenant blessing — that having gone to Jacob…yet Esau did receive a great blessing of a temporal kind…Esau thus received what he most wanted, for he cared very little for the spiritual blessing — not being a spiritual man." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

---

### vv. 10–11 — "I Have Seen Your Face Like the Face of God"

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God."** This rich phrase has prompted varied interpretation:

  1. Ellicott: "To the Hebrew the thought of God was not terrifying, and so the vision of God's face was the sight of something good and glorious. There is much of Oriental hyperbole…but it clearly conveyed the idea that Esau was using his power as generously and lovingly as is the wont of God." — (from search excerpt)

  2. The Pulpit Commentary catalogues several views: Jacob neither uses adulation, nor calls Esau a god like a heathen potentate, nor simply uses a superlative. Rather, either (a) Esau gave the same friendly welcome one would receive from God (Rosenmüller, Keil, Murphy), or (b) Jacob came into Esau's presence with the same penitence as if before God (Kalisch), or (c) as Jacob had already seen God's face at Peniel and lived, so now he has seen Esau's face and not been destroyed (Quarry). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

  3. Constable: "Jacob had seen God's gracious face and had been spared at Peniel, and he now saw Esau's gracious face and was spared." Kidner is cited: Jacob's "language shows that he saw the two encounters with his Lord and his brother, as two levels of a single event: cf. 10b with Genesis 32:30." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

  4. Gill: Jacob saw "the face of God" in that he observed "the love and favour of God to him, in working upon the heart of Esau." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **"Please accept my gift…because God has been gracious to me and I have all I need."** Jacob calls the present "my blessing" (בִּרְכָתִי). The Pulpit notes this word is used elsewhere for a gift expressing goodwill (1 Samuel 25:27; 30:26; 2 Kings 5:15). Constable suggests Jacob may have been "attempting to return to [Esau] the blessing that should have been his, to undo his sins of earlier years" (cf. Wenham). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

- **"I have all I need"** — Jacob's Hebrew (יֶשׁ־לִי־כֹל, "I have all") is stronger than Esau's "I have much" (יֶשׁ־לִי רָב). Gill notes Jacob "had besides a large share of temporal mercies, all spiritual ones; God was his covenant God…he had all grace bestowed on him, and was an heir of glory." The Pulpit says this "is regarded by some (Ainsworth) as indicating a more contented spirit than that evinced by Esau." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **"So Jacob pressed him until he accepted."** In Eastern custom, accepting a gift sealed a covenant of friendship. "If your present be received by your superior you may rely on his friendship; if it be declined you have everything to fear" (Pulpit, citing A. Clarke). Guzik: "Esau's receiving of the gifts was as important to the reconciliation as Jacob's giving of the gifts." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

---

### vv. 12–14 — "I Will Lead on Slowly"

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Let us be on our way, and I will go ahead of you."** Esau's offer to travel together or to escort Jacob. The Pulpit says it is uncertain whether Esau meant to accompany Jacob on his way (Keil, Kalisch) or invited Jacob to go with him to Mount Seir (Ainsworth, Clericus). Either way, "they amounted to an offer to be an escort." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- **"My lord knows that the children are frail, and I must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young."** Ellicott says the phrase "flocks and herds with young" (literally "giving suck") leads Thompson (*Land and Book*) to infer it was winter, since then alone the flocks are in that condition — "and thinks that this is confirmed by Jacob making folds for his cattle at Succoth." — (from search excerpt)

- Gill elaborates: "if he, and the servants under him, should push them on too fast, beyond their strength, even but one day, all in the above circumstances would be in danger of being lost through overmuch fatigue and weariness." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- **"Please let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will continue on slowly…until I come to my lord at Seir."** Guzik says: "Jacob was glad to be reconciled with his brother but didn't want to be too close to him. He was still afraid of Esau." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Matthew Henry takes a spiritualising approach: "It is not desirable to be too intimate with superior ungodly relations, who will expect us to join in their vanities, or at least to wink at them…Such will either be a snare to us, or offended with us." And draws a Christological application: "let Jacob's care and tender attention to his family and flocks remind us of the good Shepherd of our souls, who gathers the lambs with his arm, and carries them in his bosom, and gently leads those that are with young, Isaiah 40:11." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

**A Reformed Baptist Application (Piper):**

- John Piper at Desiring God uses this passage as a lesson on pastoral and fatherly leadership: "We must know whom we are leading to get our people home…Jacob enjoys fresh acceptance from Esau and blessing from God, but notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't ride off at full speed with Esau and his men. Rather, he looks back and around him and…utters words of a true shepherd." Piper applies: "Brothers, lead at a pace they can follow…'I will lead on softly.'" — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lead-at-a-pace-they-can-follow

**The Question of Deception:**

- Did Jacob ever intend to go to Seir? The Pulpit notes Calvin's view: Jacob "practiced a deception on his generous brother in order to get rid of him, by promising what he never meant to fulfill." But Gill defends Jacob: "that he should tell a lie is not likely, nor does he seem to be under any temptation to it: and besides, it would have been dangerous to have disobliged his brother when on his borders." Ellicott thinks Jacob did intend to visit but the plan was "not carried out probably because Esau did not as yet settle there, but returned to Hebron to his father." Constable says Scripture "does not record whether Jacob ever made such a trip." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

---

### vv. 15–16 — Esau Offers Men; Jacob Declines; They Part

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Let me leave some of my people with you."** Esau offers an armed escort. Jacob declines politely: "Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord."

- Gill: "Jacob saw not the necessity of it; he knew the direct way very probably; he thought himself in no danger, since he was at peace with Esau, and he did not affect the grandeur of an equipage." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests: "perhaps because, being a man of peace, he did not care for the society of soldiers, but chiefly, we apprehend, because, having Jehovah as a guide, he did not need the help of roving buccaneers (cf. Ezra 8:22)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Guzik: Jacob "was still afraid of Esau" and wanted no entanglement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Constable: "Jacob's reasons for declining Esau's offer of an escort evidently did not spring from fear. He gave a legitimate explanation…Jacob may have been counting on God's protection and therefore felt no need of Esau's men. Alternatively Jacob may have mistrusted Esau having been deceived himself and having been deceptive." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

---

### v. 17 — Jacob at Succoth

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock."** Succoth means "booths." Gill notes it was on the east side of Jordan, later belonging to the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13:27). The Targum of Jonathan says Jacob stayed there a whole year; Jarchi says 18 months — "a winter and two summers; but this is all uncertain." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- Ellicott provides a vivid picture: "Jacob…built him an house, and made booths for his cattle. This is something quite unusual, as the cattle in Palestine remain in the open air all the year round." Ellicott reconstructs: Jacob, after the exhausting flight from Laban, the terror of meeting Esau, the all-night wrestling match and the sprained hip, finally "breaks down." He "went into the corner close by, where the two rivers would both protect him and provide his cattle with water and herbage. And there he not only put up some protection…for his cattle, but built a house for himself—something, that is, more solid than a tent: and there he lay until he was healed of his lameness. The strained sinew would require some months of perfect rest before Jacob could move about." — (from search excerpt)

- The Pulpit Commentary says the interval at Succoth "appears to be imperatively required by the exigencies of the ensuing narrative concerning Dinah, who could not at this time have been much over six years of age" — she must have grown older for the events of Genesis 34 to occur. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Guzik takes a more critical view: "God had appointed Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to live in the land, but in tents as sojourners. The building of a house was disobedient and an unwise settling down." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Matthew Henry: "Jacob did not content himself with words of thanks for God's favour to him, but gave real thanks. Also he kept up religion, and the worship of God in his family." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

---

### v. 18 — Arrival at Shechem

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"After Jacob had come from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem."** The Hebrew word שָׁלֵם (Shalem) is debated. The Pulpit Commentary notes some render it as a place name (LXX, Vulgate, Syriac, Luther, Calvin, Poole, Wordsworth), but "is better taken as an adverb signifying *in peace* or *in safety*" (Onkelos, Saadias, Rashi, Dathius, Rosenmüller, Gesenius, Keil, Kalisch). It may mean Jacob was "sound in his limb" (Jarchi) and safe, no more endangered by Esau. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Ellicott: "Shalem is right, and means whole, sound…Onkelos, however, followed by most modern commentators, renders it *in peace*, but this too would not mean peaceably, but that his troubles were now at an end, and his lameness cured. Philippsohn's rendering…is 'wohlbehalten,' in good condition." — (from search excerpt)

- Gill: Jewish writers "generally understand it of his coming in peace, health, and safety." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- Guzik: "It is good Jacob came to the Promised Land, and he settled there. But he came short of full obedience because it seems God directed him to return to Bethel (Genesis 31:13). This time in Shechem would not be good for Jacob and his family." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

- Constable notes Jacob chose Shechem (meaning "peaceful") as his home — Shechem was only about a mile from the Sychar of Jesus' day (cf. John 4:5, 12). God had granted Jacob's request by bringing him safely back (cf. Genesis 28:20–21). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

---

### v. 19 — The Purchase of Land

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"The plot of ground where he pitched his tent, he purchased from the sons of Hamor…for a hundred pieces of silver."** The Hebrew word is **kesitahs** (קְשִׂיטָה). The Pulpit Commentary explains: the LXX, Vulgate, and Onkelos translate it "lambs" — "but believed to have been a certain weight now unknown, or a piece of money of a definite value, perhaps the price of a lamb (Murphy)…probably a coin stamped with the figure of a lamb (Bochart, Munter); but coined money does not appear to have been of so great antiquity (Rosenmüller, Wordsworth, Alford)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Gill notes Jacob bought the land "though he was heir of the whole country, because, as yet, the time was not come for him or his to take possession of it." The Jewish writers interpret a "meah" as the value of one penny — making 100 of them a very small sum, though Gill seems sceptical of this. Stephen in Acts 7:16 describes it as "a sum of money." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- Constable: "By purchasing land there he showed that he regarded Canaan as his permanent home and the home of his seed. The Israelites eventually buried Joseph at Shechem (Joshua 24:32)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

- This is the first piece of the Promised Land actually owned by the patriarchs — a down-payment on the promise.

---

### v. 20 — The Altar: El-Elohe-Israel

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel."** The name means "God, the God of Israel" or "Mighty God is the God of Israel."

- The Pulpit clarifies that "called it" means **named it** (not "invoked upon it" as the Vulgate renders). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-33.html

- Gill: Jacob erected the altar "to offer sacrifice upon to God, by way of thanksgiving" for all God's mercies — safe return, reconciliation with Esau, arrival in Canaan. The name was given "in memory of God's appearance to him, and of the covenant he had made with him, and of his prayer to him, and the answer of it." Gill adds: this "teaches us to give names to places and things that may put us in mind of the goodness of God unto us." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/33.htm

- Matthew Henry: "Where we have a tent, God must have an altar." Jacob dedicated it "to the honour of God, the only living and true God; and to the honour of the God of Israel, as a God in covenant with him. Israel's God is Israel's glory." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/genesis/33.htm

- Constable: "He called Yahweh 'El-Elohe-Israel' meaning, 'The mighty God is the God of Israel.' Jacob used his own new name, Israel (Genesis 32:29). He built an altar, Jacob's first, to worship God as Abraham had done at Shechem when he had first entered Canaan (Genesis 12:6–7)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-33.html

- Guzik tempers this: "The altar was good, but complete obedience was better. God wants obedience first, then sacrifice. Jacob and his family will suffer in this wasted, disobedient period" — because Jacob went to Shechem instead of Bethel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-33/

### Summary of Differing Protestant Emphases

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphasis | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Reformed Baptist (Spurgeon)** | Esau's blessing was merely temporal; Jacob's was covenantal. Esau "cared very little for the spiritual blessing." God's sovereign grace turned Esau's heart. | Guzik citing Spurgeon; Spurgeon sermon on Gen 32 |
| **Reformed Baptist (Piper/Desiring God)** | Jacob as a model of pastoral leadership: "lead on softly," know your flock, don't drive them harder than they can endure. | desiringgod.org |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik)** | Emphasis on Jacob being "conquered by God" before he could face Esau. Building a house at Succoth was disobedience — settling down instead of sojourning. Altar good, obedience better. | enduringword.com |
| **Classic Evangelical (Matthew Henry)** | Spiritualises Esau as the "superior ungodly relation" to avoid intimacy with. Sees Jacob as type of Christ the Good Shepherd. "Where we have a tent, God must have an altar." | biblehub.com/mhc |
| **Conservative Evangelical (Constable)** | Jacob's motivations vacillated between faith and old habits. God's faithfulness to His promises is the main point, not Jacob's psychology. | studylight.org/dcc |
| **Older Baptist (Gill)** | Defends Jacob against charges of deception regarding Seir. Emphasises Jacob's "I have all" as encompassing both temporal and spiritual blessings. | biblehub.com/gill |
